explanations.explanation: Yes, he says it right at the start: "I will sing and make music with all my being." All his being, friend. That's not a little hum while he's doing dishes. That's the whole man in it, and I'd be out of breath by the second line.

It's actually true. David says, "My heart is steadfast, O God; I will sing and make music with all my being." His steady heart comes first, and then everything he's got joins in. I think that's a man who is ALL in.

That's what he says: "I will praise You, O LORD, among the nations; I will sing Your praises among the peoples." He doesn't just say it once, either. Nations, then peoples, so the song goes out wide. This man is not saving his singing for a small room.

explanations.answer: In the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's a fair guess, friend, but David doesn't say it here. He says, "I will praise You, O LORD, among the nations…" Then he says it again with "…among the peoples." So the praise goes out among nations and peoples.

Zion is a nice place for a song, but David doesn't name it here. What he says is, "I will praise You, O LORD, among the nations; I will sing Your praises among the peoples." So the praise travels. It's a song with a passport.

Yes, he says, "For Your loving devotion extends beyond the heavens…" Then he adds that God's faithfulness "…reaches to the clouds." That's a lot of reach, friend. My own reach stops where the top shelf starts.

explanations.answer: To the edge of the sea
explanations.explanation: The sea doesn't show up in this verse, friend. David says God's loving devotion "…extends beyond the heavens…" And His faithfulness "…reaches to the clouds." A shoreline is much too small for what he's describing.
David doesn't name Jerusalem here. He says, "For Your loving devotion extends beyond the heavens…" That's way past any city limit. I'd say that's a distance you can't drive.
Not quite, friend. David prays, "may Your glory cover all the earth." All the earth, not one little land. His prayer is a lot bigger than just home turf.
Right, it's false. David prays, "Be exalted, O God, above the heavens; may Your glory cover all the earth." That's every corner of it. Not even a crumb gets left out.

explanations.answer: Save them with His right hand
explanations.explanation: That's it. David prays, "Respond and save us with Your right hand, that Your beloved may be delivered." He's asking for rescue, plain and simple. I think a prayer that short and clear is a good one to borrow.

explanations.answer: Give them rain for their fields
explanations.explanation: Rain would be welcome, friend, but it isn't in this psalm. David prays, "Respond and save us with Your right hand…" What he asks for is rescue. Fields never come up.

explanations.answer: Lead them back to their land
explanations.explanation: David doesn't ask that here, friend. What he says is, "Respond and save us with Your right hand, that Your beloved may be delivered." So the request is to save and deliver. Nothing about a trip home is in these words.
Not this time, friend. God's first words from His sanctuary are, "I will triumph!" That's not a warning at all. It's a declaration, and it comes right at the start.
Right, it's false. The psalm says God has spoken from His sanctuary: "I will triumph!" There's no warning in those first words. It opens with a win.
Yes, God says, "Gilead is Mine, and Manasseh is Mine…" He claims both, the region and the tribe. Nobody has to wonder whose they are. Not a single sticky note needed.
It's actually true, friend. God says, "Gilead is Mine, and Manasseh is Mine…" Both are named, and both are His. I'd say that settles it.
That's the word: "over Philistia I shout in triumph." It echoes how God opened, with "I will triumph!" The same word shows up at the start and again here in verse 9. Triumph, friend, from the top.

I can see why you'd pick it, since the verse is full of loud, big action. But the word the psalm gives is "triumph." God says, "over Philistia I shout in triumph." It matches how He began: "I will triumph!"
A shout can sound like a warning, friend. But the psalm says, "over Philistia I shout in triumph." The word is triumph. It matches what God said first: "I will triumph!"
That's it. David asks, "Who will bring me to the fortified city? Who will lead me to Edom?" Two questions, back to back, and both are about being led. I think he's asking who's got the map.

The house of God is a good place to go, friend, but David doesn't ask for it here. He asks, "Who will bring me to the fortified city?" Then he adds, "Who will lead me to Edom?" So the questions are about the fortified city and Edom.

The Jordan doesn't show up in this psalm. David asks, "Who will bring me to the fortified city? Who will lead me to Edom?" So the other place he names is a fortified city. I think he's asking who's got the directions, because I'd be asking the same thing.

Yes, he asks, "Will You no longer march out, O God, with our armies?" It comes right after, "Have You not rejected us, O God?" Those are two hard questions in a row. I think this is a man being honest with God, and he doesn't stop there.
It's true, friend. David asks, "Will You no longer march out, O God, with our armies?" He asks it right after, "Have You not rejected us, O God?" He brings the hard questions straight to God.

explanations.answer: The help of man is worthless
explanations.explanation: That's his reason: "Give us aid against the enemy, for the help of man is worthless." He's asking God for aid, and he says why in the same breath. I think that's a man who knows where to look. David says it plainly, and so does the psalm.

Chariots are a big deal in a battle, friend, but they aren't in this psalm. David asks, "Give us aid against the enemy, for the help of man is worthless." That's the reason he gives. He says the help of man is worthless.

David doesn't say that here, friend. His words are, "Give us aid against the enemy, for the help of man is worthless." The reason he gives is that the help of man is worthless. Mocking isn't mentioned in these verses.

Yes, the last line says, "With God we will perform with valor, and He will trample our enemies." Notice who does the trampling. It's God, and David's people get to be valiant alongside Him. That's a strong way to end a song that had some hard questions in the middle.
Scatter is a good guess, friend. But the psalm's last line says, "…He will trample our enemies." The word is trample. And it's God doing it.

That's close to what a lot of battle talk sounds like, friend. But David's last line says, "With God we will perform with valor, and He will trample our enemies." The word is trample, not drive out. The song ends right there.
